    O Lord.
    O Supreme Personality of Godhead, O my Lord, You have descended into the Yadu dynasty, and thus You have spent one hundred twenty-five autumns with Your devotees.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O Supreme Lord! O master! Descending in the Yadu dynasty, you have passed one hundred and twenty-five years. Śarac-chatam means one hundred years.
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, descended into the Yadu dynasty and spent 125 autumns with His devotees — His presence is the gift, not a metaphor.
    Practical Applications
    • Today, read or hear one passage about Kṛṣṇa's personal descent into the Yadu line and refuse to abstract Him into a symbol.
    • Mark on the calendar that you, like the Yadus, have a finite span with Kṛṣṇa's saṅga in this life — and spend one block of time accordingly.
    • Speak to Kṛṣṇa directly, by name, once today, the way the Yadus addressed Him as Puruṣottama and Prabho.
    Reflection Questions
    • If Kṛṣṇa actually descended and spent 125 autumns with His devotees, what in my life shows that I take that historical fact seriously?
    • Where am I treating association with Kṛṣṇa as infinite and renewable, instead of as the bounded gift the Yadus knew it to be?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Treat your four years of college, or this one season of friendships, as a Yadu-like window — bounded, not infinite — and choose one association accordingly today.
    • When a class or post tells you God is just "the universe" or "your higher self," notice the reduction and read one śloka that addresses Kṛṣṇa as Puruṣottama instead.
    • Put your phone down for the length of one āratī and address Kṛṣṇa by name, the way the Yadus addressed Him as Prabho.
    householder
    • Calculate honestly how many autumns you likely have left with your parents, spouse, or children, and let that number reshape one decision this week.
    • In family worship tonight, address Kṛṣṇa personally — by name, as Puruṣottama — so your children hear surrender directed to a Person, not a concept.
    • Refuse the workplace habit of speaking of "the universe" or "energy" when you mean Kṛṣṇa; correct it gently in your own speech first.
    senior
    • Count your remaining autumns the way the Yadus counted 125, and let that count, not your fears, govern how you spend this week.
    • Tell one younger devotee a true thing about Kṛṣṇa as a Person — not as the Self — so the personalist line passes through you intact.
    • Loosen one attachment today that assumes you have unlimited time with a particular body, relationship, or role.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the 125 autumns as poetic exaggeration rather than as the literal span of Kṛṣṇa's manifest pastimes.
    • Dissolving Puruṣottama into an impersonal Absolute, so the verse becomes about "presence" instead of about a Person.
    • Romanticizing the Yadus' association while ignoring that even they had a finite window — and so do I.
    Discussion Prompts
    • What does it change for you to address Kṛṣṇa as Puruṣottama — the Supreme Person — rather than as the Self or consciousness?
    • The Yadus had 125 autumns with Him in person; we have books, the holy name, and devotees. Is that less, equal, or in some way more — and defend your answer.
    • Where in your life are you behaving as if Kṛṣṇa's nearness is permanent and unearned, and where are you behaving as if it is precious and bounded?
    Role Play

    A senior devotee tells a new student, "Kṛṣṇa's 125 years in Dvārakā are just a story — what matters is the inner Self." The student feels something is wrong but cannot articulate why. Pair up: one plays the senior, one the student, and work through the response a Gauḍīya teacher would want the student to arrive at.

    Objections & Responses
    • 125 autumns is obviously mythological exaggeration — taking it literally is naïve.
      The Gauḍīya line receives the Bhāgavatam as historical revelation, not mythology. Kṛṣṇa's descent into the Yadu dynasty, His pastimes, and their duration are factual; treating them as symbol is precisely the impersonalism the verse resists by naming Him Puruṣottama and Prabho.
    • Why does it matter whether Kṛṣṇa is a Person? Isn't surrender to the Absolute the same either way?
      It is not the same. You cannot address, serve, or love an abstraction; the Yadus did not pray to a principle, they prayed to Him — bhavataḥ, You. Surrender becomes real only when the One you surrender to is a Person who can receive it.

    My dear Lord, there is nothing remaining at this time for Your Lordship to do on behalf of the demigods. You have already withdrawn Your dynasty by the curse of the brāhmaṇas. O Lord, You are the basis of everything, and if You so desire, kindly return now to Your own abode in the spiritual world. At the same time, we humbly beg that You always protect us. We are Your humble servants, and on Your behalf we are managing the universal situation. We, along with our planets and followers, require Your constant protection.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Support of all things! There is nothing remaining at this time for you to do on behalf of the devatās. You have almost withdrawn your dynasty by the curse of the brāhmaṇas. If you so desire, kindly return now to your supreme abode. At the same time, we humbly beg that you always protect us and the inhabitants of the planets since we are your servants. Now nothing remains to be done for the devatās. Your family has almost disappeared. Naṣṭa here means “became invisible.” Enter into Dvārakā, a form which is beyond material senses in your form as Kṛṣṇa, and enter into Vaikuṇṭha in your form as Nārāyaṇa, since you have made your appearance on earth along with all your aṁśas.
    Personal Guidance
    When your assigned work for Kṛṣṇa is finished, ask Him to return to His abode while begging His continued protection over the duties still entrusted to you.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one service Kṛṣṇa has clearly already completed through you, and stop clinging to it as though it still defines your usefulness.
    • Before any task today, pray as the demigods do: "I am Your servant managing this small situation on Your behalf — please protect me."
    • Notice when you are postponing a natural ending (a project, a role, a season) and offer that ending to Kṛṣṇa instead of resisting it.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where am I still trying to keep Kṛṣṇa "on the job" in some area of my life that He has already wrapped up, and what would it mean to let Him return?
    • In which of my responsibilities am I forgetting that I am only a vaikuṇṭha-kiṅkara — a servant managing on His behalf, not a proprietor?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an exam, a friendship season, or a campus role is clearly ending, stop dragging it out on social media and quietly thank Kṛṣṇa that His work through it is done.
    • Before a class or a difficult conversation with peers, say inwardly, "I am Your servant managing this small situation — please protect me," and watch the anxiety drop.
    • Resist the pressure to make yourself indispensable in your friend group or club; practice the demigods' humility of asking Kṛṣṇa to protect the work, not your importance in it.
    householder
    • Identify one project at work or at home that Kṛṣṇa has obviously finished through you, and consciously hand it off instead of holding on out of habit or identity.
    • When making a family decision today — finances, schooling, a move — frame it aloud as "managing on His behalf," not as something you own outright.
    • At the end of the workday, pray specifically for protection over the spouse, children, and duties still entrusted to you, the way the lokapālas pray over their planets.
    senior
    • Take stock of the roles Kṛṣṇa has clearly retired you from, and stop trying to revive them; let those services rest as completed offerings.
    • Where you still hold responsibility — for grandchildren, a community, a temple seva — speak the demigods' prayer daily: "protect us, Your humble servants."
    • Mentor a younger devotee by showing them, in your own example, how to acknowledge an ending without bitterness and how to beg protection without entitlement.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the demigods' farewell as detachment from service, when in fact they are still actively requesting protection to continue their duties.
    • Treating "return to Your own abode" as a personal license to retreat from responsibility, instead of recognizing it as Kṛṣṇa's prerogative, not ours.
    • Forgetting that even exalted servants like the lokapālas openly acknowledge dependence — and imagining that maturity in bhakti means needing Kṛṣṇa less rather than more consciously.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The demigods say there is "nothing remaining" for Kṛṣṇa to do — share an area where you sense Kṛṣṇa's work through you is finished, and one where it clearly is not, and how you tell the difference.
    • What does it mean practically to call yourself a vaikuṇṭha-kiṅkara in your current āśrama, and where does that self-understanding break down in your week?
    • The verse holds together two requests — "please leave" and "please protect us" — without contradiction. Discuss a situation where you struggled to hold both surrender and dependence at the same time.
    Role Play

    A senior devotee has led a temple project for fifteen years and feels Kṛṣṇa has clearly brought it to completion; younger devotees insist he must stay on indefinitely "because Kṛṣṇa needs him there." One student plays the senior devotee, one plays a younger devotee, one plays a guiding elder — work through how to discern, in the spirit of this verse, when a service has reached its natural conclusion while still begging Kṛṣṇa's protection for what continues.

    Objections & Responses
    • If the demigods are asking the supreme Lord to leave, this sounds like impersonalist talk dressed up — as if His presence is optional and the universe runs on its own.
      The opposite is true. They explicitly call Him akhilādhāra, the basis of everything, and beg His continued protection in the very same breath. They are not dismissing Him; they are honoring His personal mission as complete and refusing to presume on Him beyond what He has given. This is intimate servitude, not impersonalism.
    • Why would I model my prayer on demigods? I am not running planets — this verse has nothing to do with my ordinary working life.
      The verse names them as kiṅkaras, servants managing a small situation on Kṛṣṇa's behalf — exactly your position at your job, in your family, in your sādhana. Your "planet" is whatever Kṛṣṇa has put under your care. The prayer's shape — acknowledge completion, beg continued protection — fits your scale precisely.

    The Supreme Lord said: O lord of the demigods, Brahmā, I understand your prayers and request. Having removed the burden of the earth, I have executed everything that was required on your behalf.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord said: O lord of the devatās, Brahmā! I understand your prayers and request. Having removed the burden of the earth, I have executed everything that was required on your behalf.
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself declares the mission complete — the work He came to do is finished, and He receives Brahmā's request with full awareness.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you are still 'fighting battles' that Kṛṣṇa has already concluded, and consciously lay one of them down.
    • Before beginning any task, remember that Kṛṣṇa, not you, is the actual remover of burdens — and act as His instrument, not as the proprietor of the outcome.
    • Speak to Kṛṣṇa today as one who hears you fully, the way He heard Brahmā — bring Him a real request, not a polite formality.
    Reflection Questions
    • What 'burden of the earth' am I still carrying that Kṛṣṇa is signaling has already been lifted, if only I would believe Him?
    • Where in my life am I refusing to accept that a chapter is finished, because my identity is tied to the struggle rather than to Him?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Notice the 'world-fixing' weight you pick up online — the endless feed of crises you feel personally responsible for — and practice handing one specific issue back to Kṛṣṇa today instead of doom-scrolling it.
    • Before your next exam or audition, speak to Kṛṣṇa the way Brahmā did: a clear, specific request, then trust that He has heard, and walk in to do your part.
    • Refuse the campus pressure that says your worth depends on single-handedly saving something — a cause, a friend, your family's name; do your duty as His instrument, not as the hero.
    householder
    • Identify the one family burden you have been silently carrying as if you alone must solve it — a child's struggle, a parent's illness, a financial knot — and in your morning prayer, name it and offer it specifically to Kṛṣṇa.
    • At work, when a project's outcome feels existential, remember that Kṛṣṇa is the actual executor; do your hour's labor with full attention, then close the laptop without rehearsing the result.
    • Speak to your spouse this week about one shared anxiety you have been treating as 'ours to fix alone,' and together place it before Kṛṣṇa rather than recycling it across dinner conversations.
    senior
    • Look back over the decades and notice the 'burdens of the earth' you once feared would crush you that Kṛṣṇa quietly removed in His own way; let that memory become the basis of your trust now.
    • Begin loosening your grip on the projects, properties, and people you have been holding 'for their own good' — name to Kṛṣṇa that He is the real protector, and watch how your role shifts from controller to well-wisher.
    • When mentoring younger devotees or family members, refuse to position yourself as the one who must fix their lives; point them instead to the Person who has already said the work is being done.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as cosmic backstory and missing the personal force of Kṛṣṇa's first-person 'I have done it' — He speaks, He acts, He completes.
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa's work as merely symbolic of inner forces, sliding into an impersonal reading where no actual Person hears, decides, and acts.
    • Concluding that since Kṛṣṇa does the work, our effort is irrelevant — when in fact Brahmā's prayer and the devotees' participation are part of how the work gets done.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share one situation in your life where you secretly believe the burden is yours alone to remove — and let the group press you on whether that is actually true.
    • Kṛṣṇa speaks here as a Person who has heard, understood, and acted on a specific request. How does this differ from how you usually picture 'the divine,' and where does that difference make you uncomfortable?
    • If Kṛṣṇa says the work is already done, what does that mean for our activism, our reform projects, our anxieties about the state of the world — does it relieve us, indict us, or both?
    Role Play

    One student plays a devotee who is exhausted from years of trying single-handedly to 'fix' a family situation — a struggling sibling, an aging parent, a wayward child. Another plays a senior Vaiṣṇava who gently points to this verse: Kṛṣṇa has already said the burden has been lifted. Work through the conversation: where does the exhausted devotee resist, where does pride masquerade as duty, and what does it look like to actually hand the situation to Kṛṣṇa while still doing one's own part?

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa has already removed the burden of the earth, why does the world still look so burdened — wars, injustice, suffering everywhere? This sounds like wishful theology.
      Kṛṣṇa's words here address the specific mission Brahmā prayed for, not a blanket erasure of all material suffering — material existence will continue to generate burdens as long as souls choose to identify with it. What He guarantees is that He personally acts in response to sincere prayer, in His own time and way. Our work is not to verify His statement by surveying the world, but to take Him at His word in our own life and respond by taking shelter.
    • This sounds like a passive theology — Kṛṣṇa does everything, so I sit back. Isn't that exactly the spiritual bypassing modern critics warn against?
      Notice that Brahmā still prayed, the devotees still participated, and Kṛṣṇa still descended and acted through specific deeds. Acknowledging that Kṛṣṇa is the ultimate doer is not passivity — it is the correct orientation under which our effort becomes sane rather than frantic. The opposite of false proprietorship is not inactivity, it is engaged service without the delusion of being the cause.

    That very Yādava dynasty in which I appeared became greatly magnified in opulence, especially in their physical strength and courage, to the extent that they threatened to devour the whole world. Therefore I have stopped them, just as the shore holds back the great ocean.
    Purport

    The heroes of the Yadu dynasty were so powerful that even the demigods could not check them. The enthusiasm of the Yadus was unlimitedly increased by their victories in dangerous battles, and they could not be killed. Due to their martial spirit they naturally desired to establish their power over the whole world; therefore the Lord checked them and withdrew them from the earth.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Yādava dynasty which has increased in power, courage, and wealth, threatening to spread over the whole world, has been confined to Dvārakā by me, just as ocean is confined by the shore. The Yadus cannot be defeated (uddhatam) in wealth, strength and enthusiasm in fighting. They desire to spread over the world since they are unlimited in numbers, but I have confined them to Dvārakā by my inconceivable energy. Otherwise the whole of the earth planet is insufficient for them.
    Personal Guidance
    Even God-given strength becomes destructive when unchecked; Kṛṣṇa Himself draws back what He has empowered when it threatens to devour the world.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice one area today where your strength, talent, or success has begun to crowd out humility, and consciously pull it back like a shore holds the ocean.
    • Refuse to interpret an unexpected setback as mere misfortune; ask first whether Kṛṣṇa is checking an unchecked momentum in your life.
    • Speak to someone you have been overpowering by force of personality, position, or argument, and deliberately yield ground today.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life has a genuine God-given capacity grown into something that now threatens to devour those around me?
    • If Kṛṣṇa Himself withdraws what He has empowered when it turns destructive, what am I clinging to that He may already be withdrawing?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you win an argument in a friend group or online, pause and ask whether you have served truth or simply overpowered someone weaker in speech.
    • Notice a talent — academic, athletic, social — that is starting to define you so completely that humility and friendship are getting crowded out, and deliberately rein it in this week.
    • Refuse the campus myth that unchecked ambition is always virtuous; treat a closed door, a rejection, or a missed opportunity as a possible shoreline set by Kṛṣṇa.
    householder
    • Identify one domain — career, finances, parenting authority — where your strength has begun to dominate your spouse or children, and consciously withdraw force there today.
    • When a professional setback or a stalled plan arrives, refuse the reflex of doubling down; ask whether Kṛṣṇa is holding back something that was about to devour your family's inner life.
    • Speak to your children about a capacity you once pushed too far, and what you learned when it was checked, so that vīrya and śaurya in them are anchored from the start.
    senior
    • Review the strengths that defined your working life and notice which ones, if carried unchecked into this stage, would devour the peace of those around you, and quietly set them down.
    • When age, illness, or loss of influence withdraws a power you once wielded, receive it as Kṛṣṇa's shoreline rather than as humiliation, and let it deepen surrender.
    • Mentor a younger person not by transferring your dominance but by showing where you had to be checked, so they learn early what the Yādavas had to learn at the end.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as a condemnation of strength itself, instead of as a warning against strength uncoupled from Kṛṣṇa's purpose.
    • Assuming that because the Yādavas were dear to Kṛṣṇa, their power was self-justifying — and using the same logic to excuse our own excesses.
    • Treating divine checks on our momentum as obstacles to overcome by more effort, rather than as the shoreline the Lord Himself is setting.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share an instance when a strength of yours had to be checked — by circumstance, by another person, or by the Lord — and what you only understood in hindsight.
    • The Yādavas were Kṛṣṇa's own dynasty and still had to be withdrawn; what does this say about the assumption that proximity to bhakti exempts us from correction?
    • Where in our community or family do we celebrate vīrya and śaurya in ways that may already be tipping toward the very excess this verse describes?
    Role Play

    A senior member of a temple community has built a successful preaching program through sheer force of personality, but younger devotees feel steamrolled and several have quietly left. A junior devotee has been asked to raise the concern with him. Enact the conversation, with the senior devotee first defending his results and the junior devotee drawing on the image of the shore and the ocean from this verse.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa empowered the Yādavas in the first place, isn't it contradictory and even cruel for Him to then withdraw them?
      Kṛṣṇa's empowerment is never a blank cheque; it is given for His purpose, and when that purpose is fulfilled or distorted, His withdrawal is itself an act of protection — for the world and for the empowered themselves, who would otherwise be consumed by their own momentum.
    • This sounds like a religious justification for suppressing strong, capable people whenever they become inconvenient.
      The verse is not about institutions suppressing the strong; it is Kṛṣṇa speaking about His own dynasty, which no earthly power could check. The teaching is internal: each of us must learn to recognize when our own strength has begun to devour rather than serve, and welcome the shoreline rather than resent it.

    If I were to leave this world without withdrawing the overly proud members of the Yadu dynasty, the whole world would be destroyed by the deluge of their unlimited expansion.
    Purport

    Just as a tidal wave overwhelms the boundary of the shore and wreaks havoc on innocent people, similarly, there was imminent danger that the powerful Yadu dynasty might expand beyond all boundaries of social and political control. The members of the Yadu dynasty had become proud because of their apparent familial relationship with the Personality of Godhead. Although they were very religious and devoted to brahminical culture, they had become, as indicated by the word dṛptānām, affected by pride due to their relationship with Kṛṣṇa. Furthermore, due to their intense love for Kṛṣṇa, they would certainly feel such intense separation after the Lord’s departure to the spiritual world that they would become maddened and thus become an unbearable burden on the earth. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura has pointed out, however, that the earth herself, due to attachment for Kṛṣṇa, would never consider Kṛṣṇa’s own family members to be anything but a welcome burden. Still, Kṛṣṇa wanted to remove this burden. The example is given that for the pleasure of her husband a beautiful young wife may decorate herself with many golden ornaments. These ornaments constitute a painful burden for the delicate wife, but although she is willing to bear this burden, the loving husband removes the ornaments for the pleasure of his wife. So the Lord, desiring to apply the wisdom of “An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure,” took precautions to remove from the earth the burden of the Yadu dynasty.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    If I were to leave this world without withdrawing the overly proud members of the Yadu dynasty, the whole world would be destroyed by the deluge of their unlimited expansion. The Yadus have strong pride as my servants (dṛptānām). They are compared to the ocean which overruns the shore (udvelena). Though the earth planet does not consider my associates the Yadus, who follow dharma, to be a burden on the earth, I, the master of the earth, should remove this weight from the earth, just as the husband removes the ornaments of his wife who is heavy with ornaments. Though a person can easily bear the weight of something strongly desired, he cannot easily bear the weight if it is too heavy. If a greedy merchant suddenly obtains a pile of gold, he will find it difficult to bear the weight. Earth could not even bear the weight of Kṛṣṇa: sva-nigamam apahāya mat-pratijṣām ṛtam adhikartum avapluto rathasthaḥ | dhṛta-ratha-caraṇo ’bhyayāc caladgur harir iva hantum ibhaṁ gatottarīyaḥ || Giving up his own promise not to fight, and making my vow to make him fight come true, Kṛṣṇa, situated on the chariot, quickly got down and holding the wheel of a chariot, ran towards me, like a lion coming to kill an elephant, while the earth shook and his top cloth fell to the ground. SB 1.9.36
    Related lectures
    • Vishwarup Pr Hindi SB 11-06-30 - 2018-01-03
      His Grace Vishwarup Prabhu (RNS)· 2018-01-03· English
    Personal Guidance
    Even strength rooted in nearness to Kṛṣṇa can swell into dṛpta-pride; the Lord lovingly withdraws what would otherwise crush the world.
    Practical Applications
    • Name one strength of yours that has quietly turned into dṛpta-pride because of your devotional standing, and confess it before your morning prayer today.
    • Refuse to use your closeness to Kṛṣṇa, guru, or saṅga as social leverage in even one conversation today — speak as a servant, not as an insider.
    • When Kṛṣṇa withdraws something you assumed was permanent — a position, a relationship, a role — receive it as the husband gently removing the wife's heavy ornaments, not as loss.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life has my proximity to Kṛṣṇa's family — saṅga, service, lineage — become a hidden source of pride rather than humility?
    • What 'tidal wave' of my own expansion am I unwilling to see Kṛṣṇa withdraw, even though its unchecked growth would harm those around me?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Before posting about your sādhana, service, or saṅga on social media today, ask whether you are sharing Kṛṣṇa or quietly advertising your nearness to Him.
    • In your friend group or campus circle, refuse to use your spiritual identity as a status marker — drop the subtle 'we devotees' tone for one full day.
    • If an opportunity, leadership role, or relationship is suddenly taken away this term, journal it as Kṛṣṇa removing a heavy ornament rather than as failure.
    householder
    • Examine one family decision — schooling, money, in-laws — where your sense of being a 'Kṛṣṇa-conscious household' has hardened into dṛpta-pride, and re-decide it as a servant.
    • When your career, savings, or children's success starts to feel like a tidal wave you are riding, deliberately reduce one commitment so the expansion does not crush your home's bhakti.
    • Treat any unexpected loss this year — job, status in the community, a child's path diverging — as Kṛṣṇa lovingly preventing your family from becoming an unbearable burden.
    senior
    • Audit the legacy you are building — institutions, disciples, family name — and ask whether it carries the same dṛpta swelling the Yadus showed, and where it needs to be voluntarily contracted.
    • Begin handing over one position, title, or decision today, mirroring Kṛṣṇa's own willingness to withdraw what has grown too heavy for the next generation to bear.
    • Speak to younger devotees not from the height of your years near Kṛṣṇa's family of devotees, but as one preparing to be withdrawn — let mortality, not pride, set the tone of your mentoring.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as being only about the Yadus and missing that the same dṛpta-pride grows in any devotee who feels specially connected to Kṛṣṇa.
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa's withdrawal of people, prestige, or capacities as material misfortune rather than as the Lord's loving removal of an unbearable burden.
    • Concluding that brahminical culture and devotion are themselves problematic, when the verse pinpoints pride about them — not the qualities — as the real danger.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share an area where you have noticed dṛpta-pride creeping into your devotional life — and one where the rest of the group sees it more clearly than you do.
    • Discuss whether you actually believe Kṛṣṇa would withdraw something good from your life for your own welfare, or whether you secretly expect Him only to add.
    • Debate: is it more dangerous for a community to be openly worldly, or to be 'very religious and devoted to brahminical culture' while quietly proud of its connection to Kṛṣṇa?
    Role Play

    One student plays a long-standing temple devotee who has just been quietly removed from a prominent service after years of visible success; another plays a godbrother who must help them read this verse onto their own situation — not as punishment, but as Kṛṣṇa withdrawing an ornament that had grown too heavy.

    Objections & Responses
    • It sounds cruel — Kṛṣṇa engineers the destruction of His own devoted family just because they got a little proud?
      The verse and purport frame it the opposite way: the Yadus are so dear that Kṛṣṇa Himself takes responsibility for their condition, and like a loving husband removing his wife's painful golden ornaments, He spares both them and the world the weight of their unchecked expansion.
    • If even sincere, religious, Kṛṣṇa-connected people fall into dṛpta-pride, what hope is there for an ordinary practitioner like me?
      Precisely because pride can grow inside genuine devotion, the verse trains us to stay alert and surrendered; the same Kṛṣṇa who saw the danger in the Yadus is personally invested in withdrawing it from you, which is itself His mercy, not His abandonment.

    O sinless one.
    Now due to the brāhmaṇas’ curse, the annihilation of My family has already begun. O sinless Brahmā, when this annihilation is finished and I am enroute to Vaikuṇṭha, I will pay a small visit to your abode.
    Purport

    The members of the Yadu dynasty are eternal servants of the Lord; therefore Śrīla Jīva Gosvāmī has explained the word nāśaḥ, or “destruction,” as nigūḍhāyāṁ dvārakāyāṁ praveśanam ity arthaḥ: the members of the Yadu dynasty entered into the hidden or confidential Dvārakā in the spiritual world, which is not manifested here on the earth. In other words, Dvārakā, the Lord’s abode, is manifest on the earth, and when the earthly Dvārakā is apparently removed, the eternal Dvārakā in the spiritual world remains as it is. Since the members of the Yadu dynasty are eternal associates of the Lord, there is no question of their destruction. Only our conditioned vision of their manifestation was destroyed. This is the meaning of the word nāśaḥ.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Now due to the brāhmaṇa’s curse, the disappearance of my family has already begun. O sinless Brahmā, when my family disappears. I will pay a visit to your abode. Nāśaḥ means “entering into invisible Dvārakā.” After they enter Dvārakā, I will go to your abode in the form of the son of Vikuṇṭha. It actually means the planet called Vaikuṇṭha above Brahmaloka. [Note: The avatāra Vaikuṇḥta, son of Vikuṇṭhā, created a planet called Vaikuṇḥta which is situated above Brahmaloka. See Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.4.12-13. When Kṛṣna appears all the avatāras appear within him, and when he disappears they all return to their abodes. Thus Vaikuṇṭha will return to the planet Vaikuṇṭha above Brahmaloka.] This is the explanation of Jīva Gosvāmī.
    Personal Guidance
    What looks like the annihilation of Kṛṣṇa's dynasty is really their entry into eternal Dvārakā — His associates are never destroyed, only veiled from our conditioned sight.
    Practical Applications
    • When you read of the Yadus' end, refuse the materialist reading — remind yourself the destruction was only of our visible access, not of them.
    • Today, name one loss in your life (a person, a phase, a place) and ask whether what ended was the thing itself or only your conditioned view of it.
    • Before sleep, offer obeisances to the Lord's eternal associates and pray for the vision to see continuity where the senses report disappearance.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life am I treating an apparent ending as if it were a real annihilation, the way an outsider would read the Yadu-nāśa?
    • What would change in how I grieve, or how I read scripture, if I trusted that the Lord's associates and pastimes are never actually destroyed?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a friend group dissolves after school or college, resist the story that 'it's all gone' — ask what was eternal in those bonds and what was only your conditioned view of them.
    • Next time a social media account, a phase of identity, or a public version of yourself ends, sit with the difference between losing the thing and losing your access to it.
    • Pick one verse this week that disturbs you (a curse, a death, a defeat) and read Prabhupāda's purport before deciding what the verse 'really' says.
    householder
    • When you watch a parent age, a child leave home, or a career chapter close, refuse the materialist verdict that the relationship is being destroyed — pray to see what is eternal in it.
    • In family conflicts that feel like the end of something, hold the Yadu-nāśa in mind: the Lord uses apparent ruptures to relocate what is real, not to abolish it.
    • Teach your children the Jīva Gosvāmī reading of nāśaḥ the next time a pet dies or grandparents pass — give them, early, the vocabulary of concealment rather than annihilation.
    senior
    • As bodily powers and social roles fall away, rehearse this verse: what is being destroyed is the conditioned manifestation, not the soul or its eternal relationships.
    • When peers die, mentor the younger ones who are watching you — show them what it looks like to grieve without believing in annihilation.
    • Make peace, one by one, with the people and places you will soon leave behind, trusting that the Lord conceals His associates rather than ending them — and that the same logic applies to your own departure.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading the destruction of the Yadu dynasty literally and concluding that Kṛṣṇa's associates share the fate of conditioned souls.
    • Using the esoteric meaning of nāśaḥ as spiritual bypass — denying real grief in one's own life by repeating 'nothing is ever destroyed.'
    • Treating the brāhmaṇas' curse as a flaw in the līlā rather than as the Lord's chosen instrument for withdrawing His earthly manifestation.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Jīva Gosvāmī reads nāśaḥ as entry into the hidden Dvārakā — share with your partner one passage of scripture where you have been reading destruction where you should have been reading concealment.
    • Kṛṣṇa tells Brahmā He will visit his abode en route to Vaikuṇṭha — what does it say about the Lord's relationships that He announces His departure to a devotee in advance?
    • Disagree productively: is it more dangerous for a student to read the Yadu-nāśa too literally, or to leap to the esoteric reading before sitting with the apparent one?
    Role Play

    One student plays a serious newcomer who has just read SB 11.6.31 and is shaken — 'If Kṛṣṇa's own family can be destroyed by a curse, what hope is there for us?' The other plays a senior practitioner who must lead them, without dismissing the grief, into Jīva Gosvāmī's reading of nāśaḥ as entry into the hidden Dvārakā.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like a later commentator rescuing an embarrassing episode — the plain text says destruction, and Jīva Gosvāmī invents a spiritual reading to save the doctrine.
      The plain text also says Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Personality of Godhead and the Yadus are His eternal associates; if we take that plainly too, then nāśaḥ cannot mean ontological destruction without contradiction. Jīva Gosvāmī is not rescuing the verse from its meaning, he is holding two of its plain claims together — that is what a careful reader of scripture does.
    • If the destruction is only apparent, then the brāhmaṇas' curse accomplished nothing real, and the whole episode becomes theater.
      The curse accomplished exactly what the Lord wished — the withdrawal of His earthly manifestation at the appointed time. It is not theater; it is līlā, in which the Lord uses His own devotees and their words to orchestrate His coming and going. What looks like nothing real to the outside eye is the very mechanism by which He returns to Vaikuṇṭha.

    Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus addressed by the Lord of the universe, the self-born Brahmā fell down in obeisances at the lotus feet of the Lord. Surrounded by all the demigods, the great Brahmā then returned to his personal abode.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Thus addressed by the Lord of the universe, the self-born Brahmā offered respects at the lotus feet of the Lord. Surrounded by all the devatās, Brahmā then returned to his abode.
    Personal Guidance
    Having received Kṛṣṇa's instruction, even Brahmā bows and withdraws — the highest response to the Lord's word is obeisance, then quiet return to one's post.
    Practical Applications
    • After hearing or reading Kṛṣṇa's instruction today, physically offer praṇāma before standing up and moving on to anything else.
    • Notice when you receive guidance and immediately argue or analyze instead of bowing first — pause, offer obeisance, then think.
    • Return to your sva-dharma post today the way Brahmā returned to his abode — not seeking more revelation, but executing what was already given.
    Reflection Questions
    • When the Lord of the universe addresses Brahmā, Brahmā falls flat — what posture do I take when scripture or guru speaks, and what does that reveal about my estimation of the speaker?
    • Where am I lingering for more instruction when I have already been told enough to act on?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a parent, teacher, or scripture class gives you guidance you didn't want, practice the Brahmā response once this week — no argument in the moment, just acceptance and quiet return to your work.
    • Notice the urge to keep scrolling for one more opinion, one more video, one more take — at some point close the feed and return to your sva-dhāma (studies, practice, service) as Brahmā returned to his abode.
    • Before an exam or interview, offer praṇāma to Kṛṣṇa and then go execute — don't keep standing in the temple asking for more reassurance.
    householder
    • When your spouse or a senior devotee gives you correction at home, take the Brahmā posture: receive it, acknowledge it bodily if appropriate, and return to your responsibilities without a counter-argument that evening.
    • After your morning sādhana, do not linger seeking more spiritual experience — go to work, to the children, to the kitchen as Brahmā went back surrounded by the demigods to run the universe entrusted to him.
    • When making a family decision after consulting śāstra and elders, stop polling for further opinions — bow to the guidance you have and act.
    senior
    • At this stage, model the Brahmā response for those younger than you: when you receive instruction from your guru or from scripture, let your juniors see you bow first and discuss later.
    • Begin returning to your sva-dhāma — increased japa, hearing, remembrance — the way Brahmā withdrew to his own abode after his work with the Lord was complete; loosen grip on roles that are no longer yours.
    • When mentoring, resist the temptation to keep giving and giving — sometimes the most powerful teaching is to offer obeisance to Kṛṣṇa in front of the student and then quietly step back.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating obeisance as a quaint ritual rather than the bodily admission that Kṛṣṇa is the loka-nātha and I am not.
    • Hearing instruction and remaining in the audience seat — endlessly studying — instead of withdrawing to one's own abode to execute it.
    • Imagining that because Brahmā is exalted, his example of total prostration does not apply to a small student like me — in fact it applies more.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Brahmā, the creator of the universe, falls down before Kṛṣṇa — share a moment when you encountered something that made your usual self-importance feel absurd, and what you did next.
    • The verse says Brahmā returned to his own abode (sva-dhāma) after receiving instruction — discuss with your partner: what is your sva-dhāma, and are you actually living in it?
    • Is bowing down a sign of weakness, dignity, or something else entirely? Argue your position with a partner who disagrees.
    Role Play

    One student plays a senior devotee who has just given clear, uncomfortable instruction (e.g., 'stop that habit, take up this service'). The other student plays themselves receiving it. Practice the Brahmā response: no negotiation, no clever counter-question — praṇāma, acceptance, and then a calm return to one's duties. Then swap roles and debrief what felt hardest.

    Objections & Responses
    • Falling prostrate before anyone is degrading — modern adults don't grovel; we engage as equals.
      Brahmā is not an inferior groveling before a superior bully — he is a clear-eyed person acknowledging an actual fact: Kṛṣṇa is the loka-nātha, the source from whom Brahmā himself was born. Refusing to bow when bowing is appropriate is not dignity; it is the ahaṅkāra pretending the fact is otherwise. Real dignity is fitting one's posture to reality.
    • If Brahmā just bows and leaves, where is the dialogue, the questioning, the working it out? This sounds like blind obedience.
      The questioning has already happened — this verse comes at the close of an instruction Brahmā sought and received. Sincere inquiry precedes surrender; once the Lord has spoken, more debate is not deeper sādhana, it is delay. The Gauḍīya line distinguishes the inquiring phase from the executing phase, and trains us to honor both in their proper order.

    Thereafter, the Personality of Godhead observed that tremendous disturbances were taking place in the holy city of Dvārakā. Thus the Lord spoke to the assembled senior members of the Yadu dynasty as follows.
    Purport

    Muni-vāsa-nivāse kiṁ ghaṭetāriṣṭa-darśanam: there is no possibility of actual disturbances or inauspicious events in holy places inhabited by saintly persons. Thus the so-called disturbances in Dvārakā were directly enacted by the Personality of Godhead for His own auspicious purpose.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Thereafter, observing that tremendous disturbances were taking place in the city of Dvārakā, the Lord spoke to the assembled senior members of the Yadu dynasty. Disturbances took place by the desire of the Lord. It is said: ity aṅgopadiśanty eke vismṛtya prāg udāhṛtam muni-vāsa-nivāse kiṁ ghaṭetāriṣṭa-darśanam Some men proposed that the troubles were due to Akrūra’s absence, but they had forgotten the glories of the Supreme Lord, which they themselves had so often described. Indeed, how can calamities occur in a place where Lord, the residence of all the sages, resides? SB 1.57.31
    Related lectures
    • RGS SB 11-06-33-42 Hindi - Twenty-Four Guru-06
      His Holiness Radha Govinda Swami· English
    Personal Guidance
    When Kṛṣṇa Himself stages the omens, even apparent calamity in Dvārakā is His arrangement — read disturbance as His call to gather and listen.
    Practical Applications
    • When something disturbing erupts in your life today, pause before reacting and ask what Kṛṣṇa may be arranging through it.
    • Call together the senior, sober voices in your circle — family elder, guru, trusted devotee — before deciding what a disturbance means.
    • Refuse the reflex that says holy or settled environments should be free of upheaval; receive the upheaval as a summons, not a failure.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which recent 'disturbance' in my life have I been treating as random misfortune rather than as Kṛṣṇa's deliberate signal to me?
    • When the Lord speaks through unsettling omens, whom do I gather around me — the indulgent and agreeable, or the yadu-vṛddhān, the senior and sobering?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When an exam result, breakup, or friend-group fallout suddenly upends your plans, treat it as Kṛṣṇa staging a moment to speak to you, not as proof you're behind in life.
    • Before posting or venting online about a personal upheaval, first sit with one senior devotee or elder and let them help you read what just happened.
    • Refuse the campus story that a 'blessed' life means a frictionless one; receive your disturbances as invitations to grow up faster than your peers.
    householder
    • When a job loss, a child's crisis, or a sudden financial reversal hits the home, call a family council with the most sober elders before you make any large decision.
    • When your household feels like it should be a settled, dharmic Dvārakā and instead feels like one with omens, resist the urge to blame your spouse or yourself and ask together what Kṛṣṇa is arranging.
    • Speak to your children about a current family disturbance in terms of the Lord's hand in it, so they learn early to read events as messages rather than as mere misfortune.
    senior
    • Read the unmistakable utpātas of late life — a diagnosis, a friend's death, fading strength — as Kṛṣṇa convening you, the way He convened the yadu-vṛddhān, to speak and to listen.
    • Make yourself available as one of the senior, sober voices the younger generation can gather when their own Dvārakā shakes, instead of withdrawing into private worry.
    • Loosen your grip on the image of a peaceful, undisturbed final chapter, and let each disturbance now teach you to depend on Kṛṣṇa personally rather than on stable circumstances.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading every inconvenience as a personal cosmic message, instead of the specific, gathered, witness-confirmed kind of omen the verse describes.
    • Assuming a holy or devotional setting should be permanently disturbance-free, and losing faith the moment it isn't.
    • Treating Kṛṣṇa's arranged disturbances as problems to fix or escape, rather than as occasions to assemble and hear what He wants to say.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a disturbance in your own life that, in hindsight, was clearly Kṛṣṇa's arrangement — and one you still cannot read that way. What is the difference?
    • If even Dvārakā receives mahā-utpātas by the Lord's design, what does that say about our expectation that a 'good spiritual life' should look outwardly stable?
    • Who are the yadu-vṛddhān in your life — the seniors you would actually gather when something inauspicious appears — and who do you gather instead?
    Role Play

    A devotee's long-running service project in a temple community suddenly collapses — funding withdrawn, key volunteers leaving, public criticism online. They come to you convinced this proves they were never qualified to serve. Sitting with them, walk through this verse: that even in Dvārakā the Lord Himself staged the disturbances, and that the right response is not self-recrimination but gathering the seniors and asking what He is saying.

    Objections & Responses
    • Calling calamities 'arranged by God' is just a coping story — it lets believers avoid the real causes of their problems and the responsibility to fix them.
      The verse doesn't tell the Yadus to do nothing; it shows Kṛṣṇa Himself convening the elders to speak and act. Recognizing His hand behind events doesn't suspend responsibility — it changes who we consult, what we're willing to hear, and which outcome we're actually working toward. Material problem-solving without that reading just rearranges the disturbance; it doesn't read the message.
    • If Dvārakā is a holy city full of saintly persons, the very idea of inauspicious omens there is a contradiction — either the place wasn't really holy, or the omens weren't really inauspicious.
      Prabhupāda resolves precisely this in the purport: in a place inhabited by saintly persons, real inauspiciousness cannot arise, so what looked like ariṣṭa-darśana was directly enacted by the Personality of Godhead for His own auspicious purpose. The 'contradiction' dissolves once we accept that He is the doer; the form is fearsome, the substance is His will.

    The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Our dynasty has been cursed by the brāhmaṇas. Such a curse is impossible to counteract, and thus great disturbances are appearing everywhere around us.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The Supreme Lord said: Our dynasty has been cursed by the brāhmaṇas. Such a curse is impossible to counteract, and thus great disturbances are appearing everywhere.
    Personal Guidance
    Kṛṣṇa Himself acknowledges the brāhmaṇas' curse on His dynasty as uncounteractable — even the Lord honors the weight of offense to devotees.
    Practical Applications
    • Notice today where you have offended a devotee or sādhu and seek their forgiveness directly, not in your head.
    • When omens of disturbance gather in your life, read them as Kṛṣṇa's arrangement rather than random misfortune.
    • Refuse to console yourself that an offense to a brāhmaṇa is small — treat vaiṣṇava-aparādha as the most serious leak in your sādhana.
    Reflection Questions
    • Which curse-like consequence in my life am I treating as bad luck rather than tracing back to an offense I have not yet repaired?
    • If even Kṛṣṇa's dynasty was not exempt from brāhmaṇa-śāpa, where am I quietly assuming my devotional standing will shield me from the results of my own offenses?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you mock a teacher or a serious devotee in your friend group for cheap laughs, stop mid-sentence and notice the cost — this is the seed of the kind of offense this verse warns against.
    • Track one week of "random bad luck" — failed exam, friendship rupture, social media humiliation — and ask honestly whether any of it traces back to how you spoke about someone who was sincerely trying to serve Kṛṣṇa.
    • Refuse the campus habit of treating elders and brāhmaṇa-like figures as outdated; speak about them, even in private chats, the way you would want to be spoken about.
    householder
    • When disturbances cluster at home — health, money, children's troubles — sit with your spouse and ask whether any vaiṣṇava-aparādha by either of you is the unaddressed root, before chasing material fixes.
    • Train your children, by example, to never speak slightingly of devotees or brāhmaṇas at the dinner table, knowing the household carries the karmic weight together.
    • If you have offended a senior devotee in your community, go in person this week — not by message — and ask forgiveness, even if it costs your social standing.
    senior
    • Review the long arc of your life and identify any unrepaired offense to a devotee or brāhmaṇa; while you still have time, seek them out or their successors and clear it.
    • Mentor younger devotees by telling them plainly: even Kṛṣṇa's own dynasty was not spared — guard your tongue about vaiṣṇavas more carefully than your investments.
    • As bodily disturbances and losses gather around you, receive them as Kṛṣṇa's winding-up arrangement rather than as injustice, and use them to deepen surrender rather than complaint.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading this verse as fatalism — "nothing can be done" — instead of as a call to fear offense in the first place.
    • Imagining Kṛṣṇa was a passive victim of the curse rather than the supreme arranger who accepted it to wind up His pastimes.
    • Using "impossible to counteract" as an excuse not to seek forgiveness, when humble appeal to the offended devotee is the prescribed remedy.
    Discussion Prompts
    • If Kṛṣṇa's own kula could not escape a brāhmaṇa's curse, what does that tell us about the relative weight we give to social status versus devotee-respect in our own communities?
    • Share an instance when you mistook a śāpa-like consequence in your life for random misfortune — what would change if you re-read it as a structured response to offense?
    • Where in our group do we tend to soften the gravity of vaiṣṇava-aparādha, and what would tightening that look like practically?
    Role Play

    Two students play householders in a temple community. One has spoken dismissively about a senior devotee behind his back; small misfortunes are now stacking up at home — illness, financial setback, family tension. The other student must use this verse to help him see the link, resist the urge to call it coincidence, and walk him through approaching the offended devotee for forgiveness.

    Objections & Responses
    • This is just primitive curse-thinking — bad things happen, and pinning them on offended brāhmaṇas is superstition.
      The verse is spoken by Kṛṣṇa Himself about His own dynasty — He is teaching that the moral universe has structure, that conscious beings empowered by tapas can set consequences in motion, and that dismissing this as superstition only insulates us from examining how our own conduct toward devotees shapes our life.
    • If the curse was impossible to counteract even for Kṛṣṇa's family, then offense is hopeless — why bother trying to repair anything?
      Kṛṣṇa allowed the curse to stand because it served His pastime of withdrawing the Yadu dynasty; for us, the prescribed remedy is humble appeal to the offended vaiṣṇava, and the verse's terror is meant to make us fear committing the offense, not to paralyze us once we have.

    My dear respected elders, we must not remain any longer in this place if we wish to keep our lives intact. Let us go this very day to the most pious place Prabhāsa. We have no time to delay.
    Purport

    Many demigods, coming to the earth to assist Lord Kṛṣṇa in His pastimes, took birth within the Yadu dynasty and appeared as Lord Kṛṣṇa’s associates. When the Lord had completed His earthly pastimes He wanted to send these demigods back to their previous service in universal administration. Each demigod was to return to his respective planet. The transcendental city of Dvārakā is so auspicious that whoever dies there immediately goes back home, back to Godhead, but because the demigod members of the Yadu dynasty, in many cases, were not yet prepared to go back to Godhead, they had to die outside the city of Dvārakā. Thus Lord Kṛṣṇa, pretending to be an ordinary living being, said, “We are all in danger. Let us all immediately go to Prabhāsa.” In this way, by His yoga-māyā Kṛṣṇa bewildered such demigod members of the Yadu dynasty and led them away to the holy place Prabhāsa.

    Since Dvārakā is parama-maṅgala, the most auspicious place, not even an imitation of inauspiciousness can take place there. Actually, Lord Kṛṣṇa’s pastime of removing the Yadu dynasty is ultimately auspicious, but since it outwardly appeared inauspicious, it could not take place in Dvārakā; therefore Lord Kṛṣṇa led the Yadus away from Dvārakā. After having sent the demigods back to their planets, Lord Kṛṣṇa planned to return to the spiritual world, Vaikuṇṭha, in His original form and remain in the eternal city of Dvārakā.

    Śrīla Bhaktisiddhānta Sarasvatī Ṭhākura has made the following important comments on this verse. Prabhāsa is a famous holy place located near the Veraval railway station, within the region of Junagarah. In Chapter Thirty of the Eleventh Canto of Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam it is written that after hearing the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Yādavas went to the mainland from the island city of Dvārakā by means of boats and then traveled to Prabhāsa in chariots. At Prabhāsa-kṣetra they drank a beverage called maireya and became engaged in a mutual quarrel. A great battle ensued, and killing each other with hard stalks of cane, the members of the Yadu dynasty acted out the pastime of their own annihilation.

    Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, manifesting His four-armed form, sat down under a pippala tree, placing His left foot, the heel of which was colored red like the red koka-nada lotus, upon His right thigh. A hunter named Jarā, watching from the shore of the ocean at Prabhāsa, mistook the Lord’s red-colored foot to be the face of a deer and shot his arrow at it.

    At the base of that same pippala tree under which Lord Kṛṣṇa had sat there is now a temple. One mile away from the tree, on the seashore, is the Vīra-prabhaṣjana Maṭha, and it is said that from this point the hunter Jarā fired his arrow.

    In the conclusion to his work Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya, Śrī Madhvācārya-pāda has written the following purport to the mauṣala-līlā. The Supreme Personality of Godhead, in order to bewilder the demons and ensure that the word of His own devotees and of the brāhmaṇas be maintained, created a body of material energy into which the arrow was shot. But the Lord’s actual four-armed form was never touched by the arrow of Jarā, who is actually the Lord’s devotee Bhṛgu Ṛṣi. In a previous age Bhṛgu Muni had placed his foot on the chest of Lord Viṣṇu. In order to counteract the offense of improperly placing his foot on the Lord’s chest, Bhṛgu had to take birth as a degraded hunter. But even though a great devotee willingly accepts such a low birth, the Personality of Godhead cannot tolerate seeing His devotee in such a fallen condition. Thus the Personality of Godhead arranged that at the end of Dvāpara-yuga, when the Lord was winding up His manifest pastimes, His devotee Bhṛgu, in the form of the hunter Jarā, would cast the arrow into a material body created by the Lord’s illusory energy. Thus the hunter would become remorseful, gain release from his degraded birth and go back to Vaikuṇṭha-loka.

    Therefore, to please His devotee Bhṛgu and to confuse the demons, the Supreme Lord manifested His mauṣala-līlā at Prabhāsa, but it should be understood that this is an illusory pastime. The Personality of Godhead, Lord Kṛṣṇa, from His very appearance on the earth, did not manifest any of the material qualities of ordinary human beings. The Lord did not appear from the womb of His mother. Rather, by His inconceivable power He descended into the maternity room. At the time of His giving up this mortal world, He similarly manifested an illusory situation for the sake of bewildering the demons. To bewilder the nondevotees, the Lord created an illusory body out of His material energy while simultaneously remaining personally in His own sac-cid-ānanda body, and thus He manifested the downfall of an illusory material form. This pretense effectively bewilders foolish demons, but Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s actual transcendental, eternal body of bliss never experiences death.

    Also at Prabhāsa-kṣetra there is the holy place known as Bhṛgu-tīrtha, which was manifested by Lord Paraśurāma. The place at which the two rivers Sarasvatī and Hiraṇyā flow together into the ocean is named Bhṛgu-tīrtha, and there the hunter cast his arrow. There is an elaborate description of Prabhāsa-tīrtha in the Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa. There are also many phala-śrutis given within the Mahābhārata in connection with Prabhāsa-tīrtha. Phala-śrutis are scriptural statements that promise various auspicious results for one who performs a particular pious activity. In the following verses the Lord Himself will explain the particular benefits to be derived from visiting Prabhāsa-kṣetra and performing religious activities there.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    My dear respected elders! We must not remain any longer in this place if we wish to keep our lives intact. Let us go today to the most pure place Prabhāsa. We should not delay. Let Dvārakā remain with all my eternal associates! The devatās had previously entered the Yadus unseen by others. By my power of yoga I will extract them from the Yadus and take them to Prabhāsa. I will make them fight there by my māyā and send them to Svarga, and I, in my form as the son of Vikuṇṭha and as other forms as well (who were merged within me), will go to Vaikuṇṭha above Brahmaloka and other spiritual abodes. In my complete form, I, with my associates, will remain eternally in Dvārakā. This is what the Lord was thinking.
    Personal Guidance
    When Kṛṣṇa Himself signals it is time to move, do not linger — recognize His arrangement and act today, not later.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one situation where Kṛṣṇa is clearly signaling you to leave or change course, and act on it today rather than negotiating delay.
    • Stop treating "mā ciram" — no delay — as optional; when sādhana or duty calls, refuse the inner voice that says "tomorrow."
    • Speak respectfully to the elders in your life ("āryakāḥ") even when urging hard change, modeling Kṛṣṇa's tone in this verse.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in my life is Kṛṣṇa arranging an apparent danger to move me toward a more auspicious place, and how am I resisting?
    • What does it cost me — and those who follow my lead — that I keep delaying the move I already know I must make?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When a friend group, course, or online space has clearly become spiritually corrosive, leave today — do not wait for the semester or the drama to end.
    • Treat exam-season or career pivots as Kṛṣṇa's "go to Prabhāsa" moments — relocate your time and attention to where sādhana and study can actually happen.
    • When older family members or seniors resist a clearly needed change, speak to them as "āryakāḥ" — with respect and urgency, not eye-rolls or silence.
    householder
    • If your job, neighborhood, or schedule is steadily eroding family sādhana, plan and execute the move — change of city, role, or hours — without indefinite delay.
    • When you sense Kṛṣṇa rearranging your circumstances through illness, loss, or opportunity, lead your spouse and children toward the more auspicious option rather than clinging to the familiar.
    • Stop using "consulting elders" as a permanent stall; consult them properly, then act on the clear direction today, as Kṛṣṇa did with the Yadu elders.
    senior
    • Recognize that Kṛṣṇa may be quietly winding up your active pastimes too — begin loosening grip on home, role, and reputation while you can still choose the auspicious place.
    • Choose now, deliberately, where and how you wish to spend your final years and breaths — pilgrimage, association, dhāma — rather than letting circumstance decide.
    • Mentor juniors by your own willingness to move when Kṛṣṇa indicates, showing them that an elder's surrender is not stubborn rootedness but timely, undelayed response.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Reading Kṛṣṇa's apparent fear of danger here as ordinary human anxiety, missing that this is yoga-māyā arranging a transcendental purpose.
    • Using "go to a holy place" as escapism from duty rather than as Kṛṣṇa-directed relocation toward the auspicious.
    • Procrastinating on a clearly indicated change by hiding behind consultation, comfort, or false humility before elders.
    Discussion Prompts
    • Share a time when an outwardly inauspicious event in your life turned out to be Kṛṣṇa's auspicious arrangement — and one where you are still unsure.
    • Kṛṣṇa addresses His elders before moving them; discuss where authority and urgency clash in your own family or sangha, and who yields.
    • If even the Yadus had to leave Dvārakā because they were not ready to go back to Godhead, what does "readiness" mean for us — and is it our concern or Kṛṣṇa's?
    Role Play

    One student plays a senior family member resistant to leaving a comfortable but stagnant situation; another plays a younger devotee who, like Kṛṣṇa addressing the āryakāḥ, must urge an immediate move toward a more auspicious circumstance without disrespect, evasion, or delay.

    Objections & Responses
    • If Kṛṣṇa is God, why does He speak as if afraid for His life and tell everyone to flee — isn't this just an ordinary human reaction?
      Prabhupāda explains this is yoga-māyā: Kṛṣṇa pretends to be an ordinary living being to lead the demigod-Yadus, who were not yet ready to go back to Godhead, out of Dvārakā so the apparent inauspiciousness could not occur in that parama-maṅgala place.
    • Telling people to rush off to a "pious place" sounds like religious escapism — shouldn't we face our problems where we are?
      Kṛṣṇa is not advising flight from duty but obedience to His own arrangement; Prabhāsa is where He has work for them, and "mā ciram" applies whenever His direction is clear — staying put then becomes the real evasion.

    Once, the moon was afflicted with consumption because of the curse of Dakṣa, but just by taking bath at Prabhāsa-kṣetra, the moon was immediately freed from his sinful reaction and again resumed the waxing of his phases.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Once, the moon was afflicted with consumption because of the curse of Dakṣa, but just by taking bath at Prabhāsa, the moon was immediately freed from his suffering and again resumed the waxing of his phases. Just by bathing at Prabhāsa, the moon, afflicted with consumption, became freed of suffering and was able to increase its phases.
    Related lectures
    • Chaitanya Charan Pr SB 11-06-36-39 - 2017-02-28 ISKCON Alachua
      His Grace Chaitanya Charan Prabhu· 2017-02-28· English
    Personal Guidance
    Even the moon, cursed and wasting away, was restored by bathing at Prabhāsa — sacred place and surrender can dissolve reactions no self-effort can.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one "wasting" pattern in your life — a reaction that keeps depleting you — and stop trying to fix it by willpower alone; place it before Kṛṣṇa in your sādhana today.
    • Make at least one act of bathing, prasāda, or chanting today a deliberate refuge rather than a routine, the way the moon entered Prabhāsa as a desperate appeal, not a habit.
    • When you feel the slow drain of a past mistake, refuse the modern script of "just work harder on yourself" and instead approach a holy place, name, or association with the humility of one already cursed.
    Reflection Questions
    • What is the "dakṣa-śāpa" still operating in my life — a consequence I earned long ago that keeps quietly eating my phases of strength — and have I ever truly taken shelter from it, or only managed it?
    • Where do I trust my own remedies more than the purifying power of sacred place, name, and devotional bath, and what does that preference reveal about my actual faith?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • Name the one habit from school or social media that is quietly waning your energy each month, and instead of another self-improvement app, bring it into your chanting and into one visit to a temple this week.
    • When friends mock the idea of "holy places" as superstition, do not argue — quietly notice in yourself whether you actually believe Kṛṣṇa lives in His dhāma, because that belief is what the moon had and what made the bath work.
    • Stop assuming that because you are young, reactions don't accumulate yet; the moon was a demigod and still got cursed — start treating your apologies, especially to parents and teachers, with the seriousness of someone who knows offense is real.
    householder
    • Pick the one family pattern — a recurring argument, a financial leak, a parenting failure — that keeps returning each month like a waning phase, and bring it specifically into your next pilgrimage or temple visit rather than another self-help conversation.
    • When raising children, do not teach tīrtha-visits as cultural tourism; let them see you approach a holy place as the moon approached Prabhāsa — with a real problem and real dependence — so they learn the personal mood, not just the ritual.
    • If you have offended a Vaiṣṇava, a spouse, or a guru somewhere along the way, recognize that this is the kind of "dakṣa-śāpa" that quietly eats a householder's strength; seek out the dhāma and the sādhu-saṅga that can lift it, not just better time management.
    senior
    • Take inventory of long-standing reactions you have been carrying for decades — grudges, regrets, half-confessed offenses — and plan one final, serious tīrtha-yātrā specifically to lay them down, in the moon's mood, not as a sightseeing trip.
    • As your physical "phases" wane with age, refuse the modern story that decline is just biology; offer the waning itself as the moon offered his disease at Prabhāsa, and let the remaining years wax in chanting rather than in self-pity.
    • Mentor younger devotees by being concrete about which offenses cost you which phases of life, and where the dhāma and the holy name actually restored you — testimony, not theory, is what they need from you now.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating tīrtha-bathing or chanting as a magical rinse that excuses ongoing offense, instead of as Kṛṣṇa's mercy received in a mood of dependence.
    • Concluding that since the moon was freed "immediately," one's own purification should also be instant, and abandoning sādhana when results feel slow.
    • Romanticizing the verse into impersonal "sacred energy at holy sites" rather than seeing Kṛṣṇa Himself as the actual purifier acting through His dhāma.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The moon was cursed by Dakṣa for a real offense, not a misunderstanding — discuss whether we tend to minimize our own offenses (to Vaiṣṇavas, to guru, to spouse) and how that minimization blocks the kind of bath the moon took.
    • Share a time you tried to repair a long-standing reaction by self-improvement alone — what did it cost, and what would it have looked like to instead approach a holy place or holy name in the moon's mood?
    • Is there a difference between going to a tīrtha as a tourist, as a seeker of relief, and as one who knows Kṛṣṇa personally resides there — and which mode actually describes our last pilgrimage?
    Role Play

    A student tells the teacher: "I've been chanting for ten years, I visit the dhāma every year, and yet an old habit from before I took up bhakti still drains me every month — I feel like the waning moon. What am I doing wrong?" The teacher must respond using only this verse — neither dismissing the student's frustration nor promising instant relief, but locating the missing ingredient the moon brought to Prabhāsa.

    Objections & Responses
    • This sounds like superstition — bathing in a particular river cannot literally cure a disease or erase karma; it's pre-scientific thinking dressed up as devotion.
      The verse is not claiming a chemical property of water; it is showing that Kṛṣṇa has personally invested certain places with His purifying potency, and that when a soul approaches such a place in a mood of helpless dependence, the reaction He had sanctioned can be lifted by the same authority that imposed it. The cure is personal, not mechanical — which is precisely why it cannot be replicated in a laboratory and is not meant to be.
    • If a single bath at Prabhāsa frees the moon "immediately," then morality is cheap — anyone can offend and then just visit a tīrtha to wipe it clean.
      The moon did not stroll in casually; he came under a curse from Dakṣa, in visible decay, with nowhere else to turn — that is the qualification the verse quietly assumes. Cheap purification requires cheap remorse, which Kṛṣṇa does not honor; the tīrtha works for those who arrive as the moon did, not as tourists hedging their offenses.

    By bathing at Prabhāsa-kṣetra, by offering sacrifice there to placate the forefathers and demigods, by feeding the worshipable brāhmaṇas with various delicious foodstuffs and by bestowing opulent gifts upon them as the most suitable candidates for charity, we will certainly cross over these terrible dangers through such acts of charity, just as one can cross over a great ocean in a suitable boat.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    By bathing at Prabhāsa, by offering tarpanas to the Pitṛs and devatās, by feeding the worshipable brāhmaṇas with various delicious foodstuffs and by bestowing gifts upon them as the most suitable candidates for charity, like sowing seeds, we will certainly cross over these terrible dangers through such acts of charity, just as one can cross over a great ocean in a suitable boat. We will feed the attractive (uśijaḥ) brāhmaṇas with food (andhasā). Just as on sowing seeds in a fertile field one obtains many fruits, so by giving charity to qualified candidates, we will obtain great results.
    Personal Guidance
    Cross life's terrible dangers as one crosses an ocean by boat — through pilgrimage, offering to forefathers, and feeding worthy brāhmaṇas with śraddhā.
    Practical Applications
    • Identify one 'worshipable' recipient today — a sincere devotee or brāhmaṇa — and feed them or serve them with care, not as a transaction but as offering.
    • Set aside a fixed portion of this month's income for dāna placed in a suitable pātra, refusing the impulse to scatter it on unworthy causes that feel good.
    • Before any act of charity today, pause and place śraddhā in the heart first — give nothing mechanically, give nothing without faith in Kṛṣṇa behind the act.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where have I been treating my own efforts and savings as the 'boat' that will carry me across life's dangers, rather than dāna offered with śraddhā to suitable recipients?
    • Who in my life is a genuine pātra for charity, and how have I quietly avoided giving to them because they ask nothing of me in return?
    For Each Age Group
    youth
    • When you next have spare money from a stipend or part-time job, give a small fixed portion to a devotee or temple feeding program before you spend it on yourself or friends.
    • Notice how you 'give' attention on social media — to whom, and why — and ask whether those recipients are pātra or just loud; redirect some of that attention toward a sincere practitioner you know.
    • Refuse the campus reflex that every cause with a hashtag deserves your support equally; learn to discriminate suitable recipients without becoming cynical about giving itself.
    householder
    • Build dāna into the family budget as a fixed line item — not leftovers, not impulse — and decide together with your spouse which suitable recipients receive it this year.
    • Take your children with you when you give to a brāhmaṇa, devotee, or temple kitchen, so they learn early that the 'boat' across life's ocean is built with śraddhā, not net worth.
    • When a relative's death or anniversary comes, do not let the occasion pass into mere sentiment — perform a concrete act of charity in their name, directed toward a suitable pātra.
    senior
    • Review your will and your monthly giving with this verse in hand: are the recipients suitable pātra who will carry your charity across, or convenient names that asked at the right moment?
    • Use your remaining years to mentor a younger devotee in the discrimination of pātra — what you have learned about who is a true recipient is itself a form of dāna.
    • As attachments to property and savings loosen, deliberately direct portions toward feeding devotees and brāhmaṇas, treating each gift as boat-building for the crossing now visibly ahead.
    Common Pitfalls
    • Treating charity as a self-improvement project — measuring the giver's growth instead of the recipient's suitability.
    • Giving generously to causes that flatter our modern sensibilities while neglecting the brāhmaṇas and devotees the verse names as pātra.
    • Performing the outer acts — pilgrimage, feeding, gifts — without śraddhā, so the 'boat' is built but has no one steering it across.
    Discussion Prompts
    • The verse names specific recipients — forefathers, demigods, brāhmaṇas. How do we honor this specificity today without collapsing it into a generic 'give to whoever is in need'?
    • Share a time you gave dāna and felt it was wasted on an unsuitable recipient. What did that teach you about pātra that the verse here is pointing to?
    • If charity is the boat that crosses the ocean of danger, what is the ocean for you right now — and have you been trying to swim it on your own strength?
    Role Play

    A family member has just received a year-end bonus and wants to split it: half to a trending online fundraiser with viral appeal, half to a quiet local temple's brāhmaṇa-bhojana program that no one will ever post about. Two students play the family member and a Gauḍīya friend; the friend must counsel from this verse without sounding dismissive of the fundraiser, drawing out what makes a recipient a true pātra.

    Objections & Responses
    • Feeding brāhmaṇas and offering to forefathers sounds like Vedic ritualism — surely in Kali-yuga, plain harināma and giving to anyone hungry is enough.
      Harināma is indeed the yuga-dharma, but this verse is teaching the principle of pātra — that dāna placed in suitable hands with śraddhā becomes the boat that crosses the ocean. Feeding a devotee or brāhmaṇa is not Vedic nostalgia; it is recognizing that some recipients carry our charity across, and others let it sink. The form adapts to Kali-yuga; the principle does not.
    • Calling some people more 'suitable' recipients than others sounds elitist — every human being deserves charity equally.
      Indiscriminate giving feels egalitarian but is actually a refusal to discriminate, which Kṛṣṇa Himself praises in His devotees. A doctor who gives the same medicine to every patient is not compassionate, just careless. The verse is not denying anyone food; it is teaching that dāna with śraddhā placed in a genuine pātra produces a specific spiritual result — and pretending otherwise wastes both our charity and our life.
